procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 22.09.2014 of the High Court of Calcutta in CRM No. 10431 of 2014, releasing Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 on bail.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court released Respondent Nos. 1 and 2 on bail in CRM No. 10431 of 2014.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant (presumably the prosecution or a victim) appealed to the Supreme Court, aggrieved by the High Court's order granting bail to Respondent Nos. 1 and 2. The Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and remitted the matter back to the High Court for fresh consideration, emphasizing the mandatory conditions to be satisfied before granting bail in offences under s.37 of the Act.

directions: The impugned order is set aside and the matter is remitted to the High Court for fresh consideration.
It will be open to the parties to take all available contentions before the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the accused for an offence involving a commercial quantity under the NDPS Act, 1985, without considering the mandatory twin conditions laid down in Section 37 of the Act?

facts.fact: The accused were charged with an offence under the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (NDPS) Act, 1985.
The accusation involved a 'commercial quantity' of a narcotic substance, which brings the case under the purview of Section 37 of the Act.
The High Court had granted bail to the accused.

law.description: This section contains special, non-bailable provisions for certain serious offences, including those involving a 'commercial quantity'. It overrides the general bail provisions of the Code of Criminal Procedure (Cr.P.C.).

law.law_name: Mandatory Twin Conditions for Bail under Section 37
law.description: If the Public Prosecutor opposes a bail application for an offence covered by Section 37, the court cannot grant bail unless it is satisfied that two conditions are met: (1) there are reasonable grounds for believing the accused is not guilty of the offence, and (2) the accused is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.

application.reasoning: The Supreme Court noted that since the case involved a 'commercial quantity', the stringent conditions of Section 37 were applicable.
The Court examined the High Court's order and found that it had granted bail without considering or recording its satisfaction regarding the mandatory twin conditions laid down in Section 37.
The Supreme Court held that satisfying these two conditions is mandatory before granting bail in such cases, and the High Court had failed to do so.

reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was not justified in granting bail. It set aside the High Court's order and sent the matter back (remitted it) to the High Court for fresh consideration, with instructions to decide the bail application in accordance with the mandatory requirements of Section 37 of the NDPS Act.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in granting bail to the accused for an offence involving a commercial quantity under the NDPS Act, 1985, without considering the mandatory twin conditions laid down in Section 37 of the Act?
appellant_arguments: The High Court was not justified in releasing the respondents on bail without considering the mandatory twin conditions under Section 37 of the NDPS Act.

When the Public Prosecutor opposes a bail application for offences under Section 37, the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the person is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
In this case, the High Court failed to apply these mandatory requirements before granting bail.
respondent_arguments: The case is not covered under Section 37 of the NDPS Act.

The grant of bail was justified because the accused had been in custody for 203 days, the investigation was complete, the chargesheet had been submitted, and the consignment was validly imported and had been seized.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: When a court considers granting bail to a person accused of an offence under Section 37 of the NDPS Act, and the Public Prosecutor opposes the application, the court must mandatorily satisfy two conditions in addition to the normal requirements for bail: (1) there are reasonable grounds for believing that the person is not guilty of such offence, and (2) that the person is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
obiter: The question of whether a specific case is covered under Section 37 of the NDPS Act is a matter to be addressed by the High Court.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The High Court was not justified in granting bail because it failed to consider the mandatory twin conditions laid down in Section 37 of the NDPS Act. When bail for an offence involving a commercial quantity is opposed by the Public Prosecutor, the court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds to believe the accused is not guilty and is not likely to commit any offence while on bail. The Supreme Court found 'no such consideration with regard to the mandatory requirements' in the High Court's order, which rendered the grant of bail improper and necessitated a fresh consideration of the matter.
legal_tests_applied: Once the Public Prosecutor opposes a bail application for offences enumerated under Section 37 of the NDPS Act (including those involving a commercial quantity), two conditions must be mandatorily satisfied: (1) The court must be satisfied that there are reasonable grounds for believing that the person is not guilty of such offence; and (2) that person is not likely to commit any offence while on bail.
policy_considerations: The court's reasoning enforces the strict legislative policy embedded in Section 37 of the NDPS Act, which imposes stringent, non-derogable conditions for granting bail in serious drug-related offences to curb the menace of drug trafficking.
